title: Samsung LPDDR5X-PIM at Hot Chips 2026
gist: Samsung is pitching LPDDR5X-PIM, the world's first LPDDR-based processing-in-memory product, as a lower-cost/lower-power alternative to HBM for AI inference (HBM's share of AI chip component cost rose from 52% to 63% between Q1 2024 and Q4 2025); it showed a 2.28x-3.01x real-silicon speedup running Llama-3.1-8B, but the author is skeptical about adoption because memory vendors controlling both memory and compute creates a lock-in/second-sourcing problem that only a large customer mandate or JEDEC standardization can resolve.

themes.theme: The HBM cost problem PIM is meant to solve

insights.claim: HBM's share of total AI chip package component cost rose from 52 percent in Q1 2024 to 63 percent by Q4 2025, and Samsung suggests it is likely even higher now.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Quantifies how HBM has become the dominant cost driver in AI accelerator bill-of-materials, reinforcing the thesis that memory (not compute logic) is now the primary bottleneck/cost lever in AI silicon economics — a key data point for HBM supplier (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron) pricing power and margin analysis.
insights.quote: HBM now claims the majority of AI chip component spending, and that share grew from 52 percent in Q1 2024 to 63 percent by Q4 2025. It is likely higher now.

insights.claim: Samsung argues HBM delivers the bandwidth AI inference needs but at the cost of high power consumption and complex packaging, and that the path to lower cost runs through a new memory form factor — processing-in-memory (PIM) — rather than more HBM stacking.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Positions PIM as a structurally different cost curve than HBM scaling, which if adopted could reduce hyperscaler capex growth tied to ever-more HBM stacks per accelerator — worth tracking as a potential dampener on HBM volume growth if it gains traction.
insights.quote: HBM delivers the bandwidth AI inference needs, but with high power consumption and complex packaging. Samsung argues the route to lower cost runs through a new memory form factor the LP-PIM.
insights.locator: The Need for New Memory Solutions

insights.claim: Samsung has been developing PIM since at least 2021 (starting with the Aquabolt-XL HBM2-PIM proof of concept), with LPDDR5X-PIM in 2026 marking productization as the world's first LPDDR-based PIM solution — a five-year gestation from research to product.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A multi-year R&D timeline from proof-of-concept to shipping product suggests PIM adoption, even if compelling, will be a slow-moving structural shift rather than a near-term catalyst for memory market disruption.
insights.quote: Samsung traces its PIM timeline, from the Aquabolt-XL HBM2-PIM proof of concept in 2021 through LPDDR5X-PIM productization in 2026 as the world's first LPDDR-based PIM solution.

insights.claim: LPDDR5X-PIM embeds 16 PIM blocks directly in the DRAM banks with parallel MAC trees and an ALU supporting both floating-point and integer data types, achieving 614 GB/s of PIM bandwidth at the x64 9600 Mbps operating point — eight times the 76.8 GB/s available via the conventional DRAM side of the same package.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: An 8x bandwidth multiplier from compute-in-memory versus conventional DRAM access is a dramatic efficiency gain for memory-bandwidth-bound inference workloads, directly relevant to modeling inference cost-per-token if adopted at scale.
insights.quote: PIM bandwidth reaches 614 GB/s at the x64 9600 Mbps operating point, eight times the 76.8 GB/s available on the conventional DRAM side.

insights.claim: LPDDR5X-PIM ships in a JEDEC-standard 561-ball package with 16GB across four dies per rank, targeting server, mobile, and client segments, and is the first LP-PIM product with multi-precision data type support (15 selectable MAC precision combinations, e.g. SINT4 weights for 2.4 TOPS or FP8 for ~1.2 TFLOPs per package).
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Multi-precision flexibility and a standard JEDEC package footprint lowers integration friction versus a fully bespoke memory interface, which matters for whether OEMs/hyperscalers can adopt it without redesigning their memory controllers.
insights.quote: This specification figure shows a JEDEC-standard 561-ball package with 16 GB across four dies per rank, targeting server, mobile, and client.

insights.claim: LPDDR5X-PIM achieves drop-in compatibility with a conventional DRAM controller (no new controller required) via an 'Address Align Mode' that maps DRAM addresses directly to MAC instructions, and switches between single-bank and multi-bank PIM operation faster and more reliably than the prior HBM-PIM approach.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Compatibility with existing DRAM controllers substantially lowers the integration barrier for chip designers versus requiring a custom memory controller — a key factor in whether PIM sees faster real-world adoption than prior HBM-PIM generations.
insights.quote: This mapping between DRAM addresses and MAC instructions lets LPDDR5X-PIM work with a conventional DRAM controller rather than requiring a new one.
insights.locator: How PIM Utilizes Conventional DRAM Controller

insights.claim: In a validated silicon test running Llama-3.1-8B (320-token context, SINT8 activations/SINT4 weights/SINT32 output) on Samsung's edge AI accelerator SoC, LPDDR5X-PIM finished the run in 5.4 seconds versus 12.3 seconds on conventional LPDDR5X — a 2.28x speedup — while output throughput rose to 81.3 tokens/second from 27.0, a 3.01x gain.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This is a concrete, silicon-validated (not just simulated) performance proof point on a real open-weight LLM, giving investors a hard comparison point for evaluating whether PIM-based memory could meaningfully cut edge/small-model inference latency and cost versus conventional DRAM.
insights.quote: This LPDDR5X-PIM build finished the run in 5.4 seconds against 12.3 seconds on conventional LPDDR5X, a 2.28x gain, and output climbed to 81.3 tokens per second from 27.0, a 3.01x gain.

insights.claim: Samsung is bundling software support alongside the hardware — a simulator and datasheet available on request, an SDK with reference tooling — while LPDDR6-PIM is already moving toward a finalized JEDEC LP6-PIM specification.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Active JEDEC standardization work on a next-gen LPDDR6-PIM spec signals Samsung is trying to build an industry-standard ecosystem rather than keep PIM proprietary — a meaningful step toward broader adoption and second-sourcing viability.
insights.quote: the SDK bundles reference tooling, while LPDDR6-PIM moves toward a finalized JEDEC LP6-PIM specification.

themes.theme: Adoption risk: the vendor lock-in problem

insights.claim: The author is skeptical that PIM will see organic broad adoption, arguing instead that a large customer will need to mandate and implement it before it gets widely adopted — a top-down forcing function rather than bottom-up market pull.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This is a direct, actionable prediction: watch for a single major hyperscaler or AI chip vendor design win as the real catalyst for PIM adoption, rather than expecting gradual market-wide uptake — a useful signpost for tracking whether the technology inflects commercially.
insights.quote: This one feels like one where a large customer is going to have to come in and say this is needed, implement it, and then it will get widely adopted.

insights.claim: The author raises a contrarian structural concern: giving a memory vendor control over both the memory and the compute (via PIM) increases that vendor's leverage over customers, and true adoption requires standardization so that a second source can exist — otherwise it entrenches single-vendor lock-in.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This is the key risk factor for any customer (hyperscaler, chip vendor) considering PIM: without JEDEC-level standardization enabling multiple suppliers, adopting PIM could concentrate supply chain risk with Samsung specifically — a critical due-diligence point for anyone evaluating PIM-dependent product roadmaps.
insights.quote: Perhaps the challenge is that if you give a memory vendor not just control over the memory but also the compute side, they have more leverage with their customers. You need standardization at least so a vendor can second source.
